chapterTitle: Building a Simple DApp Frontend (Putting it all together)
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 20-minute comprehensive live coding video. Start with a quick overview of the `Greeter.sol` contract and its deployment to Ganache. Then, transition to building the `index.html` DApp step-by-step.
1.  **Initial Setup (5 min):** Show the HTML structure, CSS, and basic JavaScript setup.
2.  **Wallet Connection (5 min):** Implement `connectWallet()`, demonstrating connecting MetaMask, displaying account/network, and handling `accountsChanged`/`chainChanged` events. Show how the UI updates.
3.  **Read Operations (5 min):** Implement `fetchGreeting()`, showing how to read the initial greeting and update it on refresh.
4.  **Write Operations & Events (5 min):** Implement `setGreeting()`. Demonstrate entering a new message, triggering the MetaMask confirmation, showing "pending" status, and then the real-time UI update from the `GreetingUpdated` event listener after confirmation. Highlight gas estimation and error handling (e.g., empty greeting, or a simulated revert).
Use a split-screen view: code editor on the left, browser DApp on the right. Include visual overlays for ABI/Address placeholders and security warnings. End with a challenge for learners to add a "disconnect" button and implement a `payable` function with Ether transfer.

---

screens.title: Putting a Simple DApp Frontend Together
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to combine wallet connection, provider initialization, contract reads and writes, transaction monitoring, and event-driven UI updates into a single, working DApp frontend. We use a minimal Greeter contract that stores and updates a greeting message so you can focus on integration patterns rather than complex contract logic. You will see why detecting the wallet early, providing clear user feedback, estimating gas, and listening for contract events are essential to a good experience. A common mistake is assuming the blockchain behaves like a local database; transactions are asynchronous, can revert, and cost gas, so the UI must guide the user through pending and final states. By the end of this chapter you will understand the DApp lifecycle, be able to wire Ethers. js into a simple H T M L/C S S/JavaScript UI, and design feedback that keeps users informed and safe. Think about how you would explain a pending transaction to a non-technical user and what minimal details they need to continue confidently.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to concrete, testable skills you will practice while building the Greeter frontend. First, you will integrate Ethers. js with a basic H T M L and JavaScript UI so the app can read and write contract state. Second, you will manage provider and wallet connection lifecycles, handling account and network changes gracefully. Third, you will implement transaction flows with gas estimation, pending state feedback, and event listeners so the UI updates reliably after confirmations. Finally, you will apply frontend best practices for Web3: clear error messages, disabled controls during pending operations, and parsing revert reasons for meaningful feedback. Each objective is practical: for example, connecting the wallet requires requesting accounts and instantiating a Web3 provider. Handling transaction feedback requires both optimistic UI state and event-driven reconciliation. These are the exact skills employers expect when building production-ready DApps, and practicing them here will make your next project safer and easier to debug.

Learning Objectives
Skills to build and ship a minimal Greeter DApp frontend.
Bloom: Learn → Understand → Apply → Master

Integrate Ethers.js

Wire a provider and signer to the UI so the app can read and write contract state. This matters because it forms the connection between browser wallets and your contract.

Verified Competency Milestone

Request accounts, react to accountsChanged and chainChanged, and reinitialize provider/contract. This prevents stale or misleading UI when the user switches networks or accounts.

Verified Competency Milestone

Estimate gas, disable controls during pending state, wait for confirmation, and refresh state after mining. This gives users confidence and prevents duplicate transactions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Implementation Focus
screens.narratorSegment: This second set of objectives focuses on concrete implementation and validation steps. You will initialize a Web3Provider and Contract instance correctly so write operations use the user's signer. You will create a reliable pattern for reading initial state, refreshing it, and for listening to contract events to update the UI without polling. You will implement defensive UI behaviors: disable input during pending transactions, show concise pending and confirmed messages, and re-enable controls after confirmation or error. Finally, you will practice parsing error objects and revert messages to provide actionable feedback. For example, when a transaction reverts with an ownership check, the DApp should display 'Only owner can set greeting' rather than a generic failure. These objectives are practical: complete them by wiring the provided index. html template, replacing the ABI and address, and testing against Ganache. Focus on clear messages and predictable transitions between states for the best user experience.

keyIdea.title: Implementation tasks
keyIdea.text: Initialize provider and contract with signer, design event-driven UI updates, and implement defensive UX patterns for reliability.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Implementation Focus
Implementation Tasks
Replace ABI/address, connect wallet, read state, send transactions, and handle events.
Provider & Signer

Create Ethers.js Web3Provider from window.ethereum, then call getSigner for write methods. This ensures transactions are signed by the connected account.

Contract Instance

Instantiate new Contract with ABI, address, and signer for state-changing calls; use provider for read-only calls when no signer is needed.

Event Listeners

Attach listeners for events like GreetingUpdated to refresh UI without polling, and remove listeners on disconnect to avoid duplicates.

Defensive UX

Disable controls during transactions, show concise messages, and parse revert reasons to provide actionable feedback instead of vague errors.

screens.title: DApp Lifecycle — Step-by-step
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable DApp lifecycle keeps UI and blockchain state synchronized. Start by detecting whether a Web3 wallet is available; if not, show an instructive message that a wallet is required. Next request account access to obtain the user's address. After the user approves, initialize a provider and a signer with Ethers. js, and create a Contract instance with the contract ABI and address connected to the signer so write calls are possible. Immediately read initial contract state, such as the greeting, and render it. Enable user inputs, but guard them: disable the update action during pending transactions. When the user submits a state-changing transaction, estimate gas, send the transaction, and show a pending message with the transaction hash. Attach an event listener for GreetingUpdated so the UI updates when the event fires, and wait for the transaction receipt to mark the operation confirmed. Finally, handle account or network changes by reinitializing the provider and contract. A common misconception is to treat a transaction as instantaneous; always design for pending and confirmed states with explicit transitions. How will you represent a pending state in a small UI?

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle checklist
keyIdea.text: Detect wallet → request account → init provider/signer → instantiate contract → read state → enable interaction → send tx → monitor/confirm → reconcile UI.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › DApp Lifecycle
Lifecycle Steps
  1. Detect wallet — show install instructions when absent.
  2. Connect wallet — request accounts and capture the address.
  3. Init provider & contract — create Web3Provider, signer, and Contract instance.
  4. Read initial state — fetch greeting and render it.
  5. Enable UI — allow user input but guard controls.
  6. Send tx and monitor — estimate gas, send tx, await receipt.
  7. Listen to events — update UI on GreetingUpdated.
Concrete example
When a user clicks to set a new greeting, disable the input, estimate gas, send the transaction, and show: "Transaction sent: 0xabc... Waiting for confirmation." After the receipt arrives and the event fires, update the greeting text and re-enable controls.
Common Mistake
Assuming immediate state change. Transactions are mined later; you must reflect pending and confirmed states separately.
Key Takeaway

Design explicit transitions for pending and confirmed transaction states and reconcile with events to keep UI consistent.

screens.title: Detecting and Connecting a Wallet
screens.narratorSegment: Detecting a wallet is the first defensive step in any DApp. The presence of window. ethereum indicates a compatible wallet like MetaMask, but absence should not be treated as an error; it is an opportunity to guide the user. A simple informative message asking the user to install MetaMask and why it is required reduces confusion. When window. ethereum exists, request accounts using the appropriate method that returns a promise. If the user rejects, handle the rejection and show a clear message that the connection was cancelled. After approval, capture the primary account, display it, and initialize an Ethers. js Web3Provider. One pitfall is auto-connecting without permission; always request explicit approval. Another is assuming the first account will never change; listen for accountsChanged and chainChanged and reinitialize provider, signer, and contract when those events occur. For example, if the user switches to a test network, update the chain ID shown and inform the user. Reliable detection and connection patterns prevent stale or misleading UI and make subsequent contract interactions predictable. Detecting and Connecting a Wallet means check for window.ethereum, ask for account permission, and handle user rejection while setting up a provider only after consent.. In practical terms, how to detect metamask and request account access safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Check for window.ethereum, ask for account permission, and handle user rejection while setting up a provider only after consent.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Wallet Connection
Detect Wallet
Show an instructional message if no wallet is found. If present, explain why permission is required before trying to read accounts.
Check
if (typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined') { /* wallet present */ }
Request
Call eth_requestAccounts and handle user rejection code 4001 with a friendly message.
Pitfall
Automatically assuming approval leads to silent failures. Always request explicit consent before creating a signer.
Example UI text
Display wallet status, account address shorthand, and network name. If disconnected, show: "Wallet not connected — click connect to continue." If MetaMask is not installed, suggest installation with a short instruction.
Key Takeaway

Request explicit wallet permission and listen for account and chain changes to keep your app in sync with the user's wallet state.

screens.title: Initialize Provider, Signer, and Contract
screens.narratorSegment: After receiving wallet permission, the next step is to initialize the objects that let your frontend talk to the blockchain. Create a Web3Provider from window. ethereum. From that provider obtain the signer; the signer represents the connected account and is used for any function that changes state. Use the contract ABI and deployed address to create a Contract instance. Pass the signer to the contract constructor when you intend to perform write operations. If you only need read-only access, you may use the provider alone and avoid requiring signatures. One practical pattern is to store both a provider-backed contract and a signer-backed contract: the former for safe reads and the latter for submits. When the account or chain changes, reinstantiate the provider and signer and create a fresh contract to avoid mismatched contexts. An easy mistake is to reuse a stale signer after an account change; doing so leads to failed transactions and confusing user feedback. Keeping initialization centralized and idempotent simplifies recovery from network and account changes. Initialize Provider, Signer, and Contract means use a provider for reads, a signer for writes, and reinitialize both on account or network changes to avoid stale contexts.. In practical terms, correctly wiring ethers.js to enable reads and writes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use a provider for reads, a signer for writes, and reinitialize both on account or network changes to avoid stale contexts.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Provider & Contract
Initialization Pattern
Create provider, then signer, then contract. Keep a small helper that returns fresh instances so you can call it on account/chain change.
Pattern
  1. Create Web3Provider with window.ethereum.
  2. Get signer via provider.getSigner().
  3. Instantiate new Contract(address, ABI, signer) for writes.
Concrete example
// Pseudo code
const provider = new ethers.providers.Web3Provider(window.ethereum);
const signer = provider.getSigner();
const greeter = new ethers.Contract(CONTRACT_ADDRESS, CONTRACT_ABI, signer);
// Use greeter.getGreeting() for reads and greeter.setGreeting() for writes
Pro tip
Keep a reinit function that tears down old listeners and recreates provider, signer, and contract on chain or account events.

screens.title: Reading Contract State
screens.narratorSegment: Reading contract state is usually straightforward because view functions do not consume gas and return immediately through the provider. In the Greeter example, call the getGreeting or greeting view function and render the returned string. Consider network latency and possible exceptions: a provider error or misconfigured contract address will fail the read. Use try…catch to detect errors and display a helpful message like 'Error fetching greeting' with a suggested action. If you use both a signer-backed contract and a provider-backed contract, prefer the provider for reads to avoid requiring the user to sign or approve unnecessary operations. Also provide a manual refresh control so users can request the latest state on demand. A common misconception is that reads always match pending transactions; if a transaction is pending but not yet mined, a subsequent read will still return the pre-transaction state. Use events and receipts to detect when to refresh the displayed greeting. For example, after a transaction receipt or GreetingUpdated event, call your read function to reconcile UI with chain state. Reading Contract State means use view functions via provider for reads, handle errors gracefully, and refresh state on events or after receiving a transaction receipt.. In practical terms, fetch the current greeting and show it reliably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Reading State
Read pattern
Call view functions with a provider-backed contract and handle errors. Offer a Refresh control and reconcile state when events arrive.
Example
const greeting = await greeterContract.getGreeting(); setGreetingText(greeting);
Misconception
Assuming a read will reflect a pending transaction. Reads only show mined state; use events and receipts to confirm changes.
Example UI block
"Hello, World!"
Show a short success or error line when fetch completes. If fetch fails, include an action like "Check network or contract address."
Key Takeaway

Read contract state via provider, use try…catch, and refresh after events or receipts to keep the UI accurate.

screens.title: Sending Transactions & Gas Estimation
screens.narratorSegment: Sending a state-changing transaction requires attention to gas and user experience. Before sending, estimate gas for the transaction using the contract's estimateGas helper. Add a small buffer to the estimated gas to reduce the chance of running out of gas. When the user triggers the action, disable the control to avoid duplicate submissions and show a clear pending message including the short transaction hash. Send the transaction via the signer-backed contract and await the transaction object, then call wait on the transaction to obtain the receipt. During this window, update the UI to indicate pending and then confirmed states. Always wrap sends and waits in try…catch so you can catch user rejections, network errors, and on-chain reverts. Parse known error shapes: user rejection has a recognizable code, while reverts often include a reason string. Provide a helpful message and re-enable controls only after you know the final state. A common error is not estimating gas and relying on defaults, which can cause out-of-gas failures or overly large costs. Estimation plus a small buffer is the recommended compromise for reliability. Sending Transactions & Gas Estimation means always estimate gas, add a buffer, disable ui during pending transactions, and await the receipt to confirm success or failure.. In practical terms, prepare, estimate, and submit a transaction safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Always estimate gas, add a buffer, disable UI during pending transactions, and await the receipt to confirm success or failure.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Transactions & Gas
Transaction steps
  1. Validate input and disable the control.
  2. Estimate gas and add a safety buffer.
  3. Send transaction and show pending status with tx hash.
  4. Await receipt and update UI on success or failure.
Example
const estimatedGas = await greeter.estimateGas.setGreeting(newGreeting); const gasLimit = estimatedGas.add(20000); const tx = await greeter.setGreeting(newGreeting, { gasLimit }); const receipt = await tx.wait();
UI notes
Show a short hash snippet for traceability and explain that confirmations may take time. When a transaction is pending, prevent duplicate submissions and explain next steps to the user.
Error case
If a transaction reverts, parse the revert reason and display it. Remember the user still paid gas up to the revert point.
Key Takeaway

Estimate gas, disable inputs during pending operations, show a concise pending message, and await receipts to confirm completion.

screens.title: Listening for Events & Updating the UI
screens.narratorSegment: Events are the most efficient way to keep a DApp synchronized without polling. The Greeter contract emits GreetingUpdated when the message changes. Attach a listener to the contract that receives the updater address, oldGreeting, and newGreeting. When the event fires, update the displayed greeting and show a success message that includes a readable short address and the new text. Make sure to avoid attaching duplicate listeners: remove or reattach listeners when reinitializing the contract on account or network change. Also consider the ordering of receipts and events: the event may arrive at the same time as the transaction receipt or slightly after, so design your handler to be idempotent. For reliability, after receiving either a receipt or event, re-run your read function to confirm on-chain state. A common misconception is that events are authoritative without the receipt; always use the receipt and event together to reconcile state and confirm inclusion. Proper event handling removes the need for repeated polling and makes your app feel real-time without unnecessary network load. Listening for Events & Updating the UI means attach event listeners for greetingupdated to refresh ui, avoid duplicate listeners, and reconcile events with receipts for accuracy.. In practical terms, use contract events to keep the frontend in sync after transactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Events & UI
Event handler pattern
Register a listener for GreetingUpdated that updates the greeting display and shows a confirmation message. Remove or reattach listeners during reinit to avoid multiple firings.
Example Listener
greeterContract.on('GreetingUpdated', (updater, oldGreeting, newGreeting) => { setGreetingText(newGreeting); showStatus(`Greeting updated by ${updater.substring(0,6)}...`); });
UI behavior
When an event arrives, update the UI and optionally animate the change. Use idempotent updates so duplicate events do not cause flicker or inconsistent state.
Misconception
Treating events as a replacement for receipts. Use both: receipts confirm inclusion, events communicate content.
Key Takeaway

Use events to update the UI in near real-time, but reconcile with receipts to ensure on-chain confirmation and avoid race conditions.

screens.title: Provider Reads vs Signer Writes
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between provider reads and signer writes is critical. A provider lets you call view functions without signing; these operations are read-only and do not cost gas. Use provider-backed contract instances for fetching status and initial data. A signer, by contrast, represents an account capable of signing transactions; any state-changing call requires a signer. For writes, pass the signer to the contract so the transaction is submitted from the user's account. Using a signer for reads forces the wallet to be accessible but still does not cost gas; however, using provider reads where possible reduces dependency on signing. A common confusion is to think reads are free only if you use a local node; reads through a public RPC are still read-only but may be rate-limited. Another practical pattern is to keep both a providerContract and signerContract; attempt reads with providerContract and only use signerContract for setGreeting. This separation simplifies permissions, reduces accidental prompts, and keeps the UI predictable for the user. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Provider vs Signer
Provider (reads)
  • Calls view functions, no gas required.
  • No signing prompt necessary.
  • Safe for initial state loads and refreshes.
Signer (writes)
  • Used for state-changing methods; requires signature.
  • Always builds a transaction that consumes gas.
  • Attach signer to Contract for setGreeting and similar calls.
Practical pattern
Maintain two contract references: providerContract for reads and signerContract for writes. This reduces unnecessary wallet prompts and clarifies intent in code.

screens.title: Parsing Errors and Showing Useful Messages
screens.narratorSegment: Error handling in Web3 frontends is more nuanced than typical web errors. You may encounter user rejection, RPC errors, or transaction reverts with a revert reason. Always wrap await calls in try…catch and inspect common shapes. User rejection typically has a standard code; display a short message like 'Action cancelled by user.' For reverts, libraries often expose a reason string inside the error object; show that text to the user as 'Transaction reverted: Only owner can set greeting.' If the error lacks a readable message, provide guidance such as checking the connected account or network. Log detailed errors to the console for debugging but keep messages to the user concise and actionable. Also ensure that UI controls are re-enabled after an error so the user can try again. A frequent oversight is leaving the UI in a disabled state after a failure, which increases confusion. Clear, specific error messages both reduce support load and help learners diagnose issues when following the hands-on activity. Parsing Errors and Showing Useful Messages means catch rejects and reverts, parse readable reasons when available, and provide concise next steps rather than raw error dumps.. In practical terms, turn low-level failures into helpful user feedback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Common error shapes
  • User rejection — short code, show friendly cancel message.
  • RPC/network error — suggest checking network and RPC endpoint.
  • Transaction revert — parse revert reason and show it clearly.
UI strategy
Display concise messages, re-enable controls after failures, and log technical details to console for developers. Avoid exposing raw stack traces to users.

If a revert includes 'Only owner can set greeting', display: "Transaction reverted: Only owner can set the greeting. Ensure you are connected with the owner's account." Offer a short next step rather than raw data.

screens.title: Designing Clear Transaction Feedback
screens.narratorSegment: A good DApp makes asynchronous blockchain behavior understandable. Use three clear states for transactions: pending, confirmed, and failed. When a transaction is submitted, show a short message with the truncated hash and an explanation that confirmation may take time. Disable the initiating control and optionally display a spinner or progress indicator. When the receipt arrives, replace the pending message with a confirmation that includes any useful on-chain evidence, such as the event data or a link to a transaction explorer where applicable. If the transaction fails or reverts, show the parsed revert reason and suggest corrective actions. Also avoid overloading users with low-level gas data unless they ask; keep default messaging simple and expose advanced details in an expandable area for power users. Testing these flows against Ganache during the hands-on activity helps you simulate network latency and reverts so your UI behavior becomes predictable under real conditions. Designing Clear Transaction Feedback means implement distinct pending, confirmed, and failed messages; disable controls during pending and provide concise next steps on failure.. Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Transaction UX
Message pattern
  • Pending: show short hash and an explanation.
  • Confirmed: show event data or updated state.
  • Failed: show revert reason and next steps.
Example messages
Pending: "Transaction sent: 0xabc... Waiting for confirmation."
Confirmed: "Greeting updated to 'Hi!' by 0x123..."
Failed: "Transaction reverted: Only owner can set greeting. Switch to the owner's account and try again."
Key Takeaway

Keep messaging simple, actionable, and stateful. Disable controls during pending and re-enable only after a final state is known.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to combine wallet connection, provider initialization, contract reads and writes, transaction monitoring, and event-driven UI updates into a single, working DApp frontend. We use a minimal Greeter contract that stores and updates a greeting message so you can focus on integration patterns rather than complex contract logic. You will see why detecting the wallet early, providing clear user feedback, estimating gas, and listening for contract events are essential to a good experience. A common mistake is assuming the blockchain behaves like a local database; transactions are asynchronous, can revert, and cost gas, so the UI must guide the user through pending and final states. By the end of this chapter you will understand the DApp lifecycle, be able to wire Ethers. js into a simple H T M L/C S S/JavaScript UI, and design feedback that keeps users informed and safe. Think about how you would explain a pending transaction to a non-technical user and what minimal details they need to continue confidently.

These learning objectives map to concrete, testable skills you will practice while building the Greeter frontend. First, you will integrate Ethers. js with a basic H T M L and JavaScript UI so the app can read and write contract state. Second, you will manage provider and wallet connection lifecycles, handling account and network changes gracefully. Third, you will implement transaction flows with gas estimation, pending state feedback, and event listeners so the UI updates reliably after confirmations. Finally, you will apply frontend best practices for Web3: clear error messages, disabled controls during pending operations, and parsing revert reasons for meaningful feedback. Each objective is practical: for example, connecting the wallet requires requesting accounts and instantiating a Web3 provider. Handling transaction feedback requires both optimistic UI state and event-driven reconciliation. These are the exact skills employers expect when building production-ready DApps, and practicing them here will make your next project safer and easier to debug.

This second set of objectives focuses on concrete implementation and validation steps. You will initialize a Web3Provider and Contract instance correctly so write operations use the user's signer. You will create a reliable pattern for reading initial state, refreshing it, and for listening to contract events to update the UI without polling. You will implement defensive UI behaviors: disable input during pending transactions, show concise pending and confirmed messages, and re-enable controls after confirmation or error. Finally, you will practice parsing error objects and revert messages to provide actionable feedback. For example, when a transaction reverts with an ownership check, the DApp should display 'Only owner can set greeting' rather than a generic failure. These objectives are practical: complete them by wiring the provided index. html template, replacing the ABI and address, and testing against Ganache. Focus on clear messages and predictable transitions between states for the best user experience.

A reliable DApp lifecycle keeps UI and blockchain state synchronized. Start by detecting whether a Web3 wallet is available; if not, show an instructive message that a wallet is required. Next request account access to obtain the user's address. After the user approves, initialize a provider and a signer with Ethers. js, and create a Contract instance with the contract ABI and address connected to the signer so write calls are possible. Immediately read initial contract state, such as the greeting, and render it. Enable user inputs, but guard them: disable the update action during pending transactions. When the user submits a state-changing transaction, estimate gas, send the transaction, and show a pending message with the transaction hash. Attach an event listener for GreetingUpdated so the UI updates when the event fires, and wait for the transaction receipt to mark the operation confirmed. Finally, handle account or network changes by reinitializing the provider and contract. A common misconception is to treat a transaction as instantaneous; always design for pending and confirmed states with explicit transitions. How will you represent a pending state in a small UI?

Detecting a wallet is the first defensive step in any DApp. The presence of window. ethereum indicates a compatible wallet like MetaMask, but absence should not be treated as an error; it is an opportunity to guide the user. A simple informative message asking the user to install MetaMask and why it is required reduces confusion. When window. ethereum exists, request accounts using the appropriate method that returns a promise. If the user rejects, handle the rejection and show a clear message that the connection was cancelled. After approval, capture the primary account, display it, and initialize an Ethers. js Web3Provider. One pitfall is auto-connecting without permission; always request explicit approval. Another is assuming the first account will never change; listen for accountsChanged and chainChanged and reinitialize provider, signer, and contract when those events occur. For example, if the user switches to a test network, update the chain ID shown and inform the user. Reliable detection and connection patterns prevent stale or misleading UI and make subsequent contract interactions predictable. Detecting and Connecting a Wallet means check for window.ethereum, ask for account permission, and handle user rejection while setting up a provider only after consent.. In practical terms, how to detect metamask and request account access safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

After receiving wallet permission, the next step is to initialize the objects that let your frontend talk to the blockchain. Create a Web3Provider from window. ethereum. From that provider obtain the signer; the signer represents the connected account and is used for any function that changes state. Use the contract ABI and deployed address to create a Contract instance. Pass the signer to the contract constructor when you intend to perform write operations. If you only need read-only access, you may use the provider alone and avoid requiring signatures. One practical pattern is to store both a provider-backed contract and a signer-backed contract: the former for safe reads and the latter for submits. When the account or chain changes, reinstantiate the provider and signer and create a fresh contract to avoid mismatched contexts. An easy mistake is to reuse a stale signer after an account change; doing so leads to failed transactions and confusing user feedback. Keeping initialization centralized and idempotent simplifies recovery from network and account changes. Initialize Provider, Signer, and Contract means use a provider for reads, a signer for writes, and reinitialize both on account or network changes to avoid stale contexts.. In practical terms, correctly wiring ethers.js to enable reads and writes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reading contract state is usually straightforward because view functions do not consume gas and return immediately through the provider. In the Greeter example, call the getGreeting or greeting view function and render the returned string. Consider network latency and possible exceptions: a provider error or misconfigured contract address will fail the read. Use try…catch to detect errors and display a helpful message like 'Error fetching greeting' with a suggested action. If you use both a signer-backed contract and a provider-backed contract, prefer the provider for reads to avoid requiring the user to sign or approve unnecessary operations. Also provide a manual refresh control so users can request the latest state on demand. A common misconception is that reads always match pending transactions; if a transaction is pending but not yet mined, a subsequent read will still return the pre-transaction state. Use events and receipts to detect when to refresh the displayed greeting. For example, after a transaction receipt or GreetingUpdated event, call your read function to reconcile UI with chain state. Reading Contract State means use view functions via provider for reads, handle errors gracefully, and refresh state on events or after receiving a transaction receipt.. In practical terms, fetch the current greeting and show it reliably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Sending a state-changing transaction requires attention to gas and user experience. Before sending, estimate gas for the transaction using the contract's estimateGas helper. Add a small buffer to the estimated gas to reduce the chance of running out of gas. When the user triggers the action, disable the control to avoid duplicate submissions and show a clear pending message including the short transaction hash. Send the transaction via the signer-backed contract and await the transaction object, then call wait on the transaction to obtain the receipt. During this window, update the UI to indicate pending and then confirmed states. Always wrap sends and waits in try…catch so you can catch user rejections, network errors, and on-chain reverts. Parse known error shapes: user rejection has a recognizable code, while reverts often include a reason string. Provide a helpful message and re-enable controls only after you know the final state. A common error is not estimating gas and relying on defaults, which can cause out-of-gas failures or overly large costs. Estimation plus a small buffer is the recommended compromise for reliability. Sending Transactions & Gas Estimation means always estimate gas, add a buffer, disable ui during pending transactions, and await the receipt to confirm success or failure.. In practical terms, prepare, estimate, and submit a transaction safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Events are the most efficient way to keep a DApp synchronized without polling. The Greeter contract emits GreetingUpdated when the message changes. Attach a listener to the contract that receives the updater address, oldGreeting, and newGreeting. When the event fires, update the displayed greeting and show a success message that includes a readable short address and the new text. Make sure to avoid attaching duplicate listeners: remove or reattach listeners when reinitializing the contract on account or network change. Also consider the ordering of receipts and events: the event may arrive at the same time as the transaction receipt or slightly after, so design your handler to be idempotent. For reliability, after receiving either a receipt or event, re-run your read function to confirm on-chain state. A common misconception is that events are authoritative without the receipt; always use the receipt and event together to reconcile state and confirm inclusion. Proper event handling removes the need for repeated polling and makes your app feel real-time without unnecessary network load. In practical terms, use contract events to keep the frontend in sync after transactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the difference between provider reads and signer writes is critical. A provider lets you call view functions without signing; these operations are read-only and do not cost gas. Use provider-backed contract instances for fetching status and initial data. A signer, by contrast, represents an account capable of signing transactions; any state-changing call requires a signer. For writes, pass the signer to the contract so the transaction is submitted from the user's account. Using a signer for reads forces the wallet to be accessible but still does not cost gas; however, using provider reads where possible reduces dependency on signing.
